About this Portfolio
Sumer Gupta

University of Essex



About Me
I’m Sumer Gupta, a student at the University
of Essex specializing in quantitative methods in government and
political analysis. My research interests lie at the intersection of
data science and political science, with a focus on:
Electoral behavior and voting patterns
Causal inference and experimental design
Data-driven policy analysis
Democratic representation and political inequality
Quantitative text analysis and political language


Education
University of Essex , Colchester, United
Kingdom.
Courses:
GV207 - Quantitative Political Analysis
GV300 - Advanced Quantitative Political Analysis
Focus Areas:
Statistical analysis using R
Regression analysis and modeling
Experimental design
Data visualization and communication
Causal inference


Technical Skills

Programming Languages
R - Primary language for statistical analysis
RMarkdown - Reproducible research and reporting
LaTeX - Creating high-quality and professional documents


R Packages and Libraries
Data Manipulation:
tidyverse ecosystem (dplyr,
tidyr, purrr) for developing functional and
pipe-oriented workflows for data restructuring
readr for implementing efficient data ingestion
methods for certain formats of delimited data and large
datasets.
stringr for manipulating strings and carrying out
complex pattern matches for data cleaning
Statistical Analysis:
Base R statistical functions for hypothesis testing and
distribution analysis
lm() and glm() frameworks for linear
and logistic multivariate modeling
Causal inference frameworks to estimate effects within
observational and experimental data
Data Visualization:
ggplot2 to construct layered graphics with custom
scales and publication-ready aesthetic mappings
ggiraph for interactive HTML graphs
Custom themes and styling to ensure visual consistency across
research outputs
Reproducible Research:
knitr for dynamic, data-driven report
generation
distill for building technical websites optimized
for scientific communication
postcards for creating minimalist landing pages for
professional portfolios and CVs
Text Analysis:
quanteda for corpus construction, tokenisation, and
document-feature matrices
readtext for loading raw text files into R
quanteda.textmodels for Naïve Bayes and other text
classifiers
quanteda.textstats for corpus statistics, keyness
analysis and similarity measures



Statistical Methods
Throughout my coursework, I’ve managed to develop proficiency in:
Descriptive Statistics:
Measures of central tendency and dispersion
Distribution analysis
Explanatory data analysis
Inferential Statistics:
Hypothesis testing
Confidence intervals
Statistical significance
Regression Analysis:
Linear regression
Logistic regression
Interaction effects and heterogeneity
Model diagnostics and validation
Data Visualization
Effective visual communication
Grammar of graphics principles
Publication-quality graphs and figures
Quantitative Text Analysis
Corpus construction and preprocessing
Bag-of-words representation
Document-Feature Matrices
TF-IDF weighting
Keyness Statistics
Supervised classification with Naïve Bayes
Preprocessing sensitivity analysis


About this Website
This portfolio was made using Distill for R Markdown and
Postcards.
All analyses are fully reproducible - every
visualization, statistic and table is directly generated from source
code, ensuring transparency and reproducability.

Contact
I always look forward to connecting with others working with
quantitative methods in social science! Feel free to reach out to me
through:
Email: sg23667@essex.ac.uk
Github: github.com/sumergupta15

              Welcome!
              My name is Sumer Gupta, and I’m a student at the
              University of Essex. This site is a digital repository for
              my work in quantitative political analysis, focusing on
              regression analysis and data visualization.
              
              
              Featured projects
              
              1. 2024 UK General Election Turnout Analysis
              Overview:
              This project attempted to investigate the low voter
              turnout (59.7%) across the 650 constituencies observed the
              2024 UK General Election and the factors behind them. By
              merging official candidacy data with geographical
              information, the analysis explores how voter engagement
              varies by nation and the structural “fairness” of
              representation in the British Parliament.
              Technical Skills:
              Data Wrangling: Cleaned
              the data-set, filtering out by-elections, standardized
              column naming, and calculated the registered turnout as a
              percentage of the total electorate.
              Statistical Analysis:
              Calculated measures of inequality, including the range,
              variance and standard deviation to analyse the inequality
              between constituency sizes in the UK.
              Data Visualization:
              Constructed violin plots and bar charts with 95%
              confidence intervals to compare the mean and median
              turnout across the four countries of the UK: England,
              Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Then, I developed
              faceted density plots to normalize the distribution, which
              would allow for an easier, “apples-to-apples”, comparison
              of constituency sizes despite the vastly different number
              of constituencies in each countries.
              Key Insights:
              Leaders: England
              displayed the highest median turout (60.7%), while Wales
              showed the lowest turnout (56.8%)
              Inequality:The largest
              constituency has 4.27 times more voters than the smallest,
              this calls into question the democratic principle of “one
              person, one vote”; if a country possesses a lower number
              of mean votes, then the average voter there has a greater
              voter-power. The analysis found that Welsh voters have the
              most voter-power, so on average, an MP in Wales is elected
              by a smaller voter base than an MP in any other country of
              the UK.
              Distribution: Northern
              Ireland has the most equally sized constituencies, while
              Scotland has the most unequally sized constituencies, this
              is characterized by the voters in remote and sparsely
              populated areas. This implies that Northern Ireland
              maintains a the principle of “one person, one vote” across
              its districts, while Scotland’s geography makes necessary
              significant deviations from that principle to ensure equal
              representation for more isolated communities.
              View Project →
              
              
              2. A/B Testing in Political Communication
              Overview:
              This project simulated a randomized controlled trial to
              evaluate the effectiveness of different forms of digital
              political messaging. I compared a “standard” (control)
              website homepage to an “issue-focused” (treatment) website
              homepage to investigate which homepage design more
              effectively converts website visitors into registered
              party supporters. I then estimated the causal impact of
              targeted messaging on the probability that a visitor will
              sign up as a party supporter.
              Technical Skills:
              Simulating an Experiment:
              Generated a synthetic data-set to represent website
              traffic and simulating random assignment to the control
              and treatment homepages.
              ATE Estimation: Estimated
              the average treatment effect (ATE) using a linear
              probability model (LPM).
              Interaction Modelling:
              Engineered an interaction term between the treatment and
              age of visitor to identify heterogeneous effects. This
              enabled me to determine whether the issue-focused homepage
              resonated more strongly with certain age groups.
              Data Visualization:
              Constructed a plot depicting the marginal effects of
              treatment on age to visualize how the impact of the
              homepage design diverges as voters grow older.
              Key Insights:
              Age Gap: The
              issue-focused homepage was significantly more effective
              for older website visitors, while younger visitors showed
              higher baseline engagement with the standard
              homepage.
              Targeting: The graph
              showing the treatment effect on age shows that an
              age-stratified communication strategy will be more
              efficient than a “one size fits all” strategy.
              View Project →
              
              
              3. Text Analysis of Inaugural Addresses
              Overview:
              This project applied quantitative text analysis to the
              US Presidential Inaugural Addresses from 1861 to 2021 to
              investigate whether partisan language patterns can be
              detected statistically. Using the quanteda
              ecosystem, I build a full text-as-data pipeline - from
              constructing a raw corpus to supervised classification -
              in order to predict the party affiliation of a politician
              purely from the vocabulary of their speech.
              Technical Skills:
              Corpus Construction: Built
              and annotated a corpus of 40 inaugural addresses using the
              built-in quanteda dataset, then reshaped the
              raw text into paragraph-level observations, increased the
              data points to enable a more granular statistical
              classification.
              Text Processing: Applied a
              rigorous reprocessing pipeline that involved tokenisation,
              stemming and stopward removal to convert raw prose into a
              structured Document-Feature Matrix (DFM) that is ready for
              analysis.
              Keyness Analysis: Identified
              the specific “marker words” that define partisan rhetoric
              using chi-squared keyness statistics which allowed for a
              data-driven comparison of the vocabulary most closely
              associated with Democrat versus Republican inaugural
              addresses.
              Supervised Classification:
              Trained a multinomial Naïve Bayes classifier, with Laplace
              smoothing, so that the categorisation of political text is
              automated. The predicted accuracy of the model is
              evaluated using industry-standard metrics, this include
              precision, recall and F1-score, on a test set.
              Key Insights:
              Predictive Asymmetry: While
              the model had higher precision for Republican labels, it
              showed better recall for democratic paragraphs. This
              suggests that while certain Republican markers are more
              distinct, the model captured a broader and less precise
              share of the Democrat rhetoric.
              Subtle Patterns: Even though
              keyness analysis showed distinct partisan vocabularies,
              these patterns proved to be too subtle for classification
              at the paragraph level.
              Predictive Power: The
              classifier achieved an accuracy of 58.3% which was only
              marginally better than the 55.7% “No Information Rate”.
              The p-value of 0.19 suggests that the model cannot
              reliably outperform a baseline guess on the basis of the
              most frequent party.
              View Project →

2024 UK General Election Turnout
Analysis
Sumer Gupta

University of Essex2026-02-19





Introduction
This project aims to study the UK 2024 General Election,
specifically, it investigates the low turnout across the constituencies
of the UK. It uses a data-set
obtained from the UK parliament.


1. Cleaning the Data-set
uk_raw <- read_csv("data/uk_data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
names(uk_raw) <- names(uk_raw) %>% tolower() %>% str_replace_all("\\s+", "_")

# By-elections are filtered out so that only general election constituencies remain in the data.

uk1 <- uk_raw %>% 
  filter(!`election_is_by-election`) 

# Selected columns are renamed for clarity and stored into uk2

uk2 <- uk1 %>%
  select(
    constituency = constituency_name,
    country = country_name,
    valid_votes = candidate_vote_count,
    electorate = electorate
  )

# Group the data by country and constituency

uk3 <- uk2 %>%
  group_by(country, constituency) %>%
  summarise(
    valid_votes = sum(valid_votes, na.rm = TRUE),
    electorate = max(electorate, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Calculate turnout and filter out invalid votes

uk <- uk3 %>%
  mutate(turnout_registered = 100 * valid_votes / electorate) %>%
  filter(is.finite(turnout_registered), electorate > 0)
This code processes the official data, it takes the raw data-set and
standardizes the column names for easier manipulation. After filtering
out by-elections to focus exclusively on general election results, the
script aggregates candidate-level data to determine the total valid
votes and maximum electorate for each constituency. Then, it calculates
the voter turnout as a percentage of the registered electorate;
transforming granular candidate information into a high-level
geographical summary. Finally, data integrity is maintained by removing
entries with invalid/empty entries to maintain a clean data-set that is
ready for comparative analysis


2. Visualization (A): Mean Turnout and Distribution by Country
# Calculate the standard error (se) and confidence intervals (ci)
turnout_by_country_ci <- uk %>%
  group_by(country) %>%
  summarise(mean_turnout = mean(turnout_registered, na.rm = TRUE),
            median_turnout = median(turnout_registered, 
                                    na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_turnout = sd(turnout_registered, na.rm = TRUE),
            n = n(),
            .groups = "drop") %>% 
  # summarises the mean and median turnout, standard deviation and sample size for each
  mutate(
    se = sd_turnout / sqrt(n),
    ci_lower = mean_turnout - 1.96 * se,
    ci_upper = mean_turnout + 1.96 * se
    ) #modifies the columns in the existing dataset (SE, CI bounds)


# Create the visualisation using ggplot2
# The first layer - a violin plot showing the full distribution 
ggplot(uk, aes(country, turnout_registered)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "#4884a5", alpha = 0.6, trim = FALSE, width = 1.2) +
# The second layer - the bar chart of mean turnout
  geom_col(data = turnout_by_country_ci, aes(y = mean_turnout), 
           width = 0.7, fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.8) +
# The third layer - error bars showing the confidence intervals 
  geom_errorbar(data = turnout_by_country_ci, 
                aes(y = mean_turnout, 
                    ymin = ci_lower, ymax = ci_upper),
                width = 0.2, size = 0.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Turnout (%)",
                     limits = c(0,90),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))
                     ) +
  labs(
    title = "UK 2024 General Election: Mean Turnout and Distribution by Country",
    x = "Country",
caption = "Violin plots show the full distribution of constituency turnouts; bars and errorbars show the mean and its 95% CI"
  )

This graph shows that the UK has the highest mean turnout across the
four nations of the UK during the 2024 General Election. The bar heights
represent the average turnout for each country, while the overlaid
violin plots show the density and spread of the turnout across
individual constituencies. In England, most constituencies are around
the average but in Scotland and Wales, there are a significant number of
constituencies that have below-average voter turnout. The error bars
indicate the 95% confidence intervals for the mean turnout, showing that
the estimates made are statistically robust.


3. Visualization (B): Differences in Constituency Sizes across
Nations of the UK
# Calculate the overall mean turnout for all of UK
overall_mean <- mean(uk$valid_votes)

# Create the visualisation using ggplot2
# The first layer - the density plot
ggplot(uk, aes(x = valid_votes)) +
  geom_density(aes(fill=country), alpha = 0.67) +
  # The second layer - vertical line showing the overall mean
  geom_vline(xintercept = overall_mean,
             color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  # Separate the plots by country
  facet_wrap(~ country, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "How do Constituency Sizes Differ Across the Nations of the UK",
    subtitle = "A comparison of the number of voters in each constituency \nacross England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland",
    y = "Number of Valid Votes per Constituency",
    x = "Density (How Common Each Size Is)"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

This graph shows that Northern-Ireland has the most equal-sized
constituencies, as the base of the curve covers the shortest range on
the x-axis (narrowest spread) - roughly 30,000 to 55,000 valid votes.
Whereas, Scotland has the most unequal-sized constituencies, as the base
of the curve is widest with a gradual tail that extends below 20,000
valid voters on the x-axis.
Such a density plot automatically normalizes the distribution, such
that the area under each curve sums to 1, regardless of the number of
constituencies within each country. The geom_density()
function uses the underlying computation of a kernel density estimator,
which assumes that the underlying distribution in the data is unbounded,
smooth and continuous. Such a visualization can handle the larger sample
size, as it automatically uses the number of observations to estimate
the curve. It is also good at visualizing the spread as it has a single
visual measure, so inequality can be inferred from looking at the width
of the curve at its base.

A/B Testing in Political
Communications
Sumer Gupta

University of Essex2026-02-19




library(ggplot2)

Introduction
This project simulates a randomized controlled trial (RCT) to
determine which type of digital messaging, such as a website homepage
with broad policy platforms or one with an issue-focused platform, can
be most effective in engaging with supporters. By randomly assigning
website visitors to different versions of a homepage, the experiment
isolates the causal effect of specific strategies on supporter
sign-ups.

Theoretical Framework
Every visitor has two potential outcomes, only one
of which we observe:
Y0: potential of visitor signing up after being
shown the standard (control) homepage
Y1: potential of a visitor signing up after being
shown the issue-focused (treatment) homepage.
According to the fundamental problem of causal
inference, we can never observe both Y0 and
Y1 for same person, if we show them the treatment homepage,
we would never know what would’ve happened under the control homepage,
and vice-versa.
Through a RCT, we can estimate the Average Treatment Effect
(ATE):
\[\text{ATE} = E[Y_1 - Y_0] = E[Y_1] -
E[Y_0]\]
Because of the average treatment effect, the treatment and control
groups are statistically equivalent. The difference in outcomes can then
be attributed to treatment, so E[Y1] can be estimated from
the treatment group and E[Y0] from the control group.



1. Simulating the Experiment
Experiment setup:
Sample size: 1,500 website visitors
Assignment: Random (There’s a 50% probability a
visitor will get either homepage)
Control condition: Standard homepage with broad
policy platforms
Treatment condition: Issue-focused
homepage
Outcome variable: Supporter sign-up (binary
indicator; 1 = yes, 0 = no)
Control sign-up rate: 12% (expected)
Treatment sign-up rate: 17% (expected)
There’s a reason to why this experiment is simulated, real A/B tests
would require actual website traffic, ethics approval, informed consent
considerations and longer observation periods. A simulation allows us to
control the true treatment effect, demonstrate statistical concepts more
clearly, explore the heterogeneity systematically and avoid the
practical difficulties of a real A/B test.
set.seed(123) # This ensures replicabiltiy 
n <- 1500 # Total visitors to the site

# Random treatment assessment
treatment <- rbinom(n = n, size = 1, prob = 0.5) 
# rbinom() generates random deviates from a binomial distribution, this is what allows us to simulate our A/B test. 

# Potential outcomes for each visitor
p_control <- 0.12 # 12% control sign-up rate
p_treated <- 0.17 # 17% treatment sign-up rate

Y0 <- rbinom(n = n, size = 1, prob = p_control)
Y1 <- rbinom(n = n, size = 1, prob = p_treated)

# Realized outcome - single results actually observed for each visitor, 
support_signup <- ifelse(treatment == 1, Y1, Y0)

# Create a data frame
party_ab <- data.frame(
  visitor_id = 1:n,
  treatment = treatment,
  support_signup = support_signup
)


2. Calculate the Average Treatment Effect (ATE)
We can model a logistic regression to determine how being in the
treatment group affects a visitor’s sign-up probability using
glm().
logit_model <- glm(support_signup ~ treatment, data = party_ab, family = binomial(link = "logit"))

summary(logit_model)
## 
## Call:
## glm(formula = support_signup ~ treatment, family = binomial(link = "logit"), 
##     data = party_ab)
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
## (Intercept)  -2.1512     0.1189 -18.097  < 2e-16 ***
## treatment     0.4756     0.1558   3.052  0.00227 ** 
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## (Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)
## 
##     Null deviance: 1163.0  on 1499  degrees of freedom
## Residual deviance: 1153.5  on 1498  degrees of freedom
## AIC: 1157.5
## 
## Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4
The coefficients of a logistic regression must be carefully
interpreted as they’re expressed in the scale of log-odds scale, not in
the traditional, 0-to-1, scale. So the treatment coefficient of 0.47 is
the log-probability of signing up increasing by 0.47 when moving from
control to treatment.
p_hat_control <- predict(
  logit_model, 
  newdata = data.frame(treatment = 0),
  type = "response"
)

# p_hat_control is the predicted probability of the logistic regression model that a specific visitor will sign-up if shown standard homepage 

p_hat_treated <-predict(
  logit_model, 
  newdata = data.frame(treatment = 1),
  type = "response"
)

# p_hat_treated is the predicted probability of the logistic regression model that a specific visitor will sign-up if shown the issue-focused homepage. 

# Given p_hat_control and p_hat_treated, we can calculate the ATE:

ate_logit <- p_hat_treated - p_hat_control

ate_logit
##         1 
## 0.0534603
The logistic regression model shows that the value of the ATE is
0.0535 which is 5.35 percentage points, the difference between the
percentage of people that signed up after observing the control and
treatment homepages.


3. Visualization: Treatment Effect by Age
set.seed(2024) 

# Simulate visitor ages using a normal distribution, limit them between 18 and 75 to refect a realistic electorate
party_ab$age <- round(pmin(pmax(rnorm(nrow(party_ab), mean = 40, sd = 12), 18), 75))

# Use a binomial distribution to randomly assign a "high interest" trait to 40% of the visitors 
party_ab$high_interest <- rbinom(nrow(party_ab), size = 1, prob = 0.4)

# Verify that the new data was added correctly
head(party_ab[, c("visitor_id", "treatment", "support_signup", "age", "high_interest")])
##   visitor_id treatment support_signup age high_interest
## 1          1         0              1  52             1
## 2          2         1              1  46             1
## 3          3         0              0  39             0
## 4          4         1              0  37             1
## 5          5         1              0  54             1
## 6          6         0              0  56             1
# To examine age-related heterogeneity, create a new linear model using lm()
lm_het_age <- lm(support_signup ~ treatment  * age, data = party_ab)

lm_het_age
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = support_signup ~ treatment * age, data = party_ab)
## 
## Coefficients:
##   (Intercept)      treatment            age  treatment:age  
##      0.061994       0.004307       0.001042       0.001236
The interaction coefficient is 0.001236 which shows how the treatment
affects change for each year of age. So for each additional year of age,
the treatment affect increases by 0.1236, which means that an
issue-focused homepage is marginally more effective for those visitors
who are older.
# Create a sequence of ages from 18 to 75.
age_seq <- seq(18,75, by = 1)

# Create a new sequence for displaying larger intervals
major_age <- seq(20,75, by = 15) 

# Extract coefficients from lm_het_age
treat <- coef(lm_het_age)["treatment"]
inter <- coef(lm_het_age)["treatment:age"]

# Create a data frame for the plot
marginal_effect_data <- data.frame(
  age = age_seq,
  treatment_effect = treat + (inter * age_seq)
)

# Filter the dataset to include only the rows where the visitor's age matches the 15-year intervals
interval_data <- subset(marginal_effect_data, age %in% major_age)

# Plot the marginal effect of age on treatment
ggplot(marginal_effect_data, aes(x = age, y = treatment_effect)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#F45D0B", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_segment(data = interval_data,
               aes(x = 18, xend = age,
                   y = treatment_effect, yend = treatment_effect),
               linetype = "dashed", colour = "#C84C09") +
  geom_point(data = interval_data, 
             colour = "#F45D0B", 
             size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = major_age,
                     minor_breaks = seq(15,75, by = 5),
                     limits = c(18,75),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0,0.01))
                     ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 0.1),
                     breaks = seq (0, 0.1, by = 0.01)) +
  labs(
    title = "The Effect of Issue-Focused Homepage by Age",
    subtitle = "Signup probability increases as visitors get older",
    x = "Visitor Age",
    y = "Treatment Effect (Percentage Point Increase)"
) +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#DCDCDC" ),
        panel.grid.minor = element_line(colour = "#DCDCDC")
) +
  theme_light()

This plot shows that the effectiveness of the issue-focused homepage
increases with visitor age. The upward-sloping line highlights a
positive relation between visitor age and treatment effect, so older
visitors are much more likely to influenced by issue-focused messaging
than younger ones.

Text Analysis of Inaugural Addresses
Sumer Gupta

University of Essex2026-03-29




library(quanteda)
library(quanteda.textmodels)
library(quanteda.textstats)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)
library(caret)

Introduction
A politician’s partisan identity doesn’t just shape what the
politician would say, but also shapes how they say it - the vocabulary,
tone and rhetoric employed. The US presidential inaugural address offers
fertile ground for testing this claim as they are one of the most
formally preserved political texts. By training a supervised machine
learning classifier to correctly identify the party affiliation of a US
president purely from the linguistic features of their inaugural
address.


1. Building and Exploring the Corpus
The dataset data_corpus_inaugural is directly built into
the quanteda package, containing 59 inaugural addressess
from the time of Washington (1789) to Biden (2021). However, since the
modern two-party system solidified after 1860, we can create a subset
from 1861 onwards - after which point the two-party competition between
Republican and Democrat goes on until the present.
#Load the built-in dataset

data("data_corpus_inaugural", package = "quanteda")

# Create a subset for the two-party era

modern_corpus <- data_corpus_inaugural[
  docvars(data_corpus_inaugural, "Year") >= 1861 & 
  docvars(data_corpus_inaugural, "Year") <= 2021
]

# Assign party labels using historical records.

years <- docvars(modern_corpus, "Year")


parties <- case_when(
  years %in% c(1861, 1865, 1869, 1873, 1877, 1881, 1889, 1897,
               1901, 1905, 1909, 1921, 1925, 1929, 1953, 1957,
               1969, 1973, 1981, 1985, 1989, 2001, 2005, 2017) ~ "Republican",
  years %in% c(1885, 1893, 1913, 1917, 1933, 1937, 1941, 1945,
               1949, 1961, 1965, 1977, 1993, 1997, 2009, 2013, 2021) ~ "Democrat"
)

docvars(modern_corpus, "Party") <- parties # docvars() attach party labels back to the corpus providing a digital tag of political affiliation. 

# Create a summary  of the Corpus

summary(modern_corpus)[, c("Text", "Types", "Tokens", "Sentences",
                            "Year", "President", "Party")]
##               Text Types Tokens Sentences Year  President      Party
## 1     1861-Lincoln  1075   3999       135 1861    Lincoln Republican
## 2     1865-Lincoln   360    775        26 1865    Lincoln Republican
## 3       1869-Grant   485   1229        40 1869      Grant Republican
## 4       1873-Grant   552   1472        43 1873      Grant Republican
## 5       1877-Hayes   831   2707        59 1877      Hayes Republican
## 6    1881-Garfield  1021   3209       111 1881   Garfield Republican
## 7   1885-Cleveland   676   1816        44 1885  Cleveland   Democrat
## 8    1889-Harrison  1352   4721       157 1889   Harrison Republican
## 9   1893-Cleveland   821   2125        58 1893  Cleveland   Democrat

## 11   1901-McKinley   854   2437       100 1901   McKinley Republican
## 12  1905-Roosevelt   404   1079        33 1905  Roosevelt Republican
## 13       1909-Taft  1437   5821       158 1909       Taft Republican
## 14     1913-Wilson   658   1882        68 1913     Wilson   Democrat

## 25 1957-Eisenhower   621   1907        92 1957 Eisenhower Republican

## 29      1973-Nixon   544   1995        68 1973      Nixon Republican
## 30     1977-Carter   527   1370        52 1977     Carter   Democrat
## 31     1981-Reagan   902   2781       129 1981     Reagan Republican

## 40      2017-Trump   582   1660        88 2017      Trump Republican
## 41      2021-Biden   812   2766       216 2021      Biden   Democrat
The resulting corpus contains speeches, comprising of both Democrat
and Republican addresses. Even though the count is slightly higher for
the Republican party, the distribution is balanced enough to give a
stable foundation for the model. This balance ensures that the
classifier would not simply “default” to the most frequent party,
enabling the statistical differences in vocabulary to drive the
predictions.
# Create a data frame for the plot

token_df <- data.frame(
  year = docvars(modern_corpus, "Year"),
  tokens = ntoken(modern_corpus),
  party = docvars(modern_corpus, "Party"),
  president = docvars(modern_corpus, "President")
)

# Plot the number of tokens (individual units of text)

ggplot(token_df, aes(x = year, y = tokens, colour = party)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey80", linewidth = 0.5, aes(group = 1)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Democrat" = "#2166AC", "Republican" = "#D6604D")) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", aes(group = 1), colour = "#7A2894", linetype = "dashed", se = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1860, 2025, by = 20)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Length of US Presidential Inaugural Addresses Over Time",
    subtitle = "This plot shows that the length of inaugural \nspeeches have gotten shorter over time",
    x        = "Year",
    y        = "Number of Tokens",
    colour   = "Party"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

This plot shows a clear trend, inaugural addresses have become
significantly shorter over time.


2. Preprocessing Pipeline
This preprocessing pipeline transforms the raw speeches into a
structured DFM (Document-Feature Matrix) by removing linguistic noise
and standardising vocabulary. Through isolating root words and filtering
out non-partisan “stopwords”, we can ensure that the model focuses on
the particular ideological markers that distinguish the two parties.
This pipeline goes through 5 steps
Tokenise and Clean: Break the text into individual words
while removing punctuation, numbers and symbols that don’t contribute to
ideological meaning. Splitting hyphens allows us to ensure that compound
terminology is captured by the component words.
Stemming: Through stemming words are reduced to their base
form, for example: ‘democracy’ and ‘democratic’ become ‘democraci’. This
groups related terms in order to give the model more consistent data
points.
Remove Stopwords: Filter out common English stopwords like
the, is, or at, that appear frequently but do not carry with them any
ideological or thematic weight.
Construct the DFM: Convert the list of words into a
mathematical grid where rows are speeches and columns represent word
counts - this is the main format required for machine learning.
Standardization: Convert all text to lowercase so that the
model doesn’t treat “Democracy” and “democracy” as two separate
words.
# 1. Tokenise and Clean

speech_tokens <- tokens(
  modern_corpus,
  remove_punct   = TRUE,   
  remove_numbers = TRUE,   
  remove_symbols = TRUE,   
  split_hyphens  = TRUE    
)

# 2. Stemming

speech_tokens <- tokens_wordstem(speech_tokens)

# 3. Remove Stopwords

speech_tokens <- tokens_remove(speech_tokens, pattern = stopwords("english"))

# 4. Construct the DFM

dfmat <- dfm(speech_tokens)

# 5. Standardization 

dfmat <- dfm_tolower(dfmat)


dfmat
## Document-feature matrix of: 41 documents, 4,565 features (87.57% sparse) and 4 docvars.
##                features
## docs            fellow citizen unite state complianc custom old govern appear
##   1861-Lincoln       2       7     5    27         1      1   3     19      1
##   1865-Lincoln       1       0     0     0         0      0   0      1      1
##   1869-Grant         0       4     2     4         0      0   0      4      0
##   1873-Grant         1       2     0     4         0      0   1      5      0
##   1877-Hayes         4       8     2    12         1      1   0     20      1
##   1881-Garfield      2       7     7    16         0      0   0     24      0
##                features
## docs            befor
##   1861-Lincoln      7
##   1865-Lincoln      1
##   1869-Grant        3
##   1873-Grant        3
##   1877-Hayes        2
##   1881-Garfield     2
## [ reached max_ndoc ... 35 more documents, reached max_nfeat ... 4,555 more features ]
The DFM shows that the 41 addresses are condensed into
4,565 unique word stems, this provides a high-dimensional
portrait of presidential rhetoric over 160 years. With a sparsity of
87.57%, the DFM indicates that even though the total
vocabulary is vast, each individual speech utilizes a very specific
subset of terms, this is ideal for identifying the unique linguistic
markers of each party. Each cell records how often a word stem appears
in a given speech.


3. Keyness Analysis
Keyness analysis is a principled statistical test that identifies
which word stems are most distinctively associated with each party in
their inaugural addresses. Using the textstat_keyness()
function from quanteda.textstats we compute a chi-squared
(\(\chi^{2}\)) statistic for each
feature, thereby measuring how significantly its frequency in the target
group diverges from what we would expect if the party had no impact on
word choice.
By comparing group-level frequencies, keyness analysis can tell us
which stems are used disproportionately by one party across all their
speeches.
# Compute keyness using Democrats as the target group and Republicans as reference

keyness <- textstat_keyness(dfmat,
                             target  = docvars(dfmat, "Party") == "Democrat",
                             measure = "chi2")

# Find the top 15 Democrat-distinctive and Republican-distinctive stems

top_dem <- head(keyness, 15)
top_rep <- tail(keyness, 15)

# Combine the two and label directions

plot_data <- bind_rows(
  mutate(top_dem, direction = "Democrat-distinctive"),
  mutate(top_rep, direction = "Republican-distinctive")
) %>%
  mutate(feature = reorder(feature, chi2))

# Plot the Keyness Analysis

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = feature, y = chi2, fill = direction)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.75) +
  coord_flip() +
  facet_wrap(~ direction, scales = "free") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Democrat-distinctive"    = "#2166AC",
    "Republican-distinctive"  = "#D6604D"
  )) +
  labs(
    title    = "Keyness Analysis: Most Distinctive Word Stems by Party",
    subtitle = "Chi-squared statistic; higher chi-squared statistic means more strongly associated with that party",
    x        = "Word Stem",
    y        = "Chi-squared Statistic",
    caption  = "Based on US Presidential Inaugural Addresses, 1861–2021"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.text      = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.title      = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

This keyness plot shows the substantively meaningful differences in
the vocabulary used by both parties:
Democrat-distinctive stems show that Democratic presidents reach for
the word “democraci” more than any other term. Their rhetoric centers
around collective solidarity, with words like “us”, “togeth” and
“journey”, and time, with words like “centuri”, “today” and
“generat”.
Republican-distinctive stems are notably institutional and
procedural. “law” is the strongest Republican-distinctive stem, followed
by words like “congress”, “enforce”, “administr”, “state” and
“constitut” - centering their language around the formal structures of
government and constitutional order.


4. Naïve Bayes Classification
Naïve Bayes is a generative probabilistic classifier
rooted in Bayes’ theorem:
\[P(\text{class} \mid \text{document}) =
P(\text{document} \mid \text{class}) \times
\frac{P(\text{class})}{P(\text{document})}\]
This makes two important assumptions: (1) the bag-of-words
assumption states that word order doesn’t matter, only the
frequency of a word used matters, and (2) the conditional
independence assumption states that given the party, words are
independent of each other. Both assumptions are technically false,
however, they still produce a strong performance for classification in
practice - this is true particularly for short texts wherein frequency
signals prove to be informative.
To increase the training sample from 41 documents to a more robust
dataset, one must reshape the corpus at the paragraph level. Each
paragraph of each speech becomes its own document, and inherits the
party label of its parent speech.
# Rebuild the DFM and reshape to the paragraph level

para_corpus <- corpus_reshape(modern_corpus, to = "paragraphs", use_docvars = TRUE)

para_tokens <- tokens(para_corpus,
                      remove_punct   = TRUE,
                      remove_numbers = TRUE,
                      remove_symbols = TRUE,
                      split_hyphens  = TRUE) %>%
  tokens_wordstem() %>%
  tokens_remove(stopwords("english"))

para_dfm <- dfm(para_tokens) %>% dfm_tolower()

# Check the class distribution at the paragraph level

table(docvars(para_dfm, "Party"))
## 
##   Democrat Republican 
##        677        822
# Create a new data frame that shows frequency and percentage distribution of speeches by political party.

party_counts <- as.data.frame(table(docvars(para_dfm, "Party")))
names(party_counts) <- c("Party", "Count")
party_counts$Proportion <- round(party_counts$Count / sum(party_counts$Count) * 100, 1)

# Create a plot to show the class distribution at the paragraph level
ggplot(party_counts, aes(x = Party, y = Count, fill = Party)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(Count, " (", Proportion, "%)")),
            vjust = -0.5, size = 4.5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Democrat" = "#2166AC", "Republican" = "#D6604D")) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(
    title    = "Class Distribution at Paragraph Level",
    subtitle = "There is a slight Republican majority that reflects the greater number of Republican presidents in this period",
    x = NULL, y = "Number of Paragraphs"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

Conduct a Train/Test (80/20) split to partition the data into two
parts, whre one is used to learn the model parameters (training set) and
the other is used to evaluate performance on unseen data (test set).
set.seed(42) # for reproducibility

# Define the 80/20 split ratio for training and testing

n_docs  <- ndoc(para_dfm)
n_train <- floor(0.80 * n_docs)

# Shuffle indices to avoid temporal ordering bias

idx_shuffled <- sample(seq_len(n_docs))
train_idx    <- idx_shuffled[1:n_train]
test_idx     <- idx_shuffled[(n_train + 1):n_docs]

# Partition the data into training and validation sets

dfm_train <- para_dfm[train_idx, ]
dfm_test  <- para_dfm[test_idx,  ]

# Fit the Multinomial Naïve Bayes

nb_model <- textmodel_nb(dfm_train,
                          y            = docvars(dfm_train, "Party"),
                          distribution = "multinomial",
                          smooth       = 1)  # Laplace (add-1) smoothing

summary(nb_model)
## 
## Call:
## textmodel_nb.dfm(x = dfm_train, y = docvars(dfm_train, "Party"), 
##     smooth = 1, distribution = "multinomial")
## 
## Class Priors:
## (showing first 2 elements)
##   Democrat Republican 
##        0.5        0.5 
## 
## Estimated Feature Scores:
##             fellow  citizen    unite    state complianc    custom      old
## Democrat   0.00178 0.002885 0.001657 0.001842 6.138e-05 0.0001228 0.001535
## Republican 0.00102 0.002918 0.001793 0.004781 1.406e-04 0.0002813 0.001020
##              govern    appear    befor   address   briefli     take   presenc
## Democrat   0.005156 6.138e-05 0.001289 0.0003069 1.228e-04 0.001166 0.0003683
## Republican 0.008227 3.516e-04 0.002180 0.0002813 7.031e-05 0.001195 0.0003516
##                 oath  prescrib constitut     taken   presid     enter    execut
## Democrat   0.0013504 0.0001842  0.001105 0.0007980 0.001596 0.0001228 0.0005525
## Republican 0.0007031 0.0002109  0.003023 0.0007734 0.001477 0.0006328 0.0018282
##                offic    consid necessari   present   discuss    matter
## Democrat   0.0008594 0.0003069 0.0004297 0.0005525 0.0001228 0.0003069
## Republican 0.0013711 0.0003516 0.0010899 0.0010547 0.0003867 0.0007734
##            administr   special   anxieti
## Democrat   0.0003683 0.0004297 0.0003069
## Republican 0.0016524 0.0004922 0.0002109
An important practical consideration is that the test set may contain
word stems that aren’t present in the training vocabulary, using
dfm_match() we can align the test DFM to the training
vocabulary, thereby removing unseen features and padding with zeros for
features in training that are absent from the test paragraph.
# Align the test DFM to the training vocabulary

dfm_test_matched <- dfm_match(dfm_test, features = featnames(dfm_train))

# Generate predictions

predicted_party <- predict(nb_model, newdata = dfm_test_matched)
actual_party <- docvars(dfm_test_matched, "Party")

predicted_party

The classifier’s accuracy is 58.3%, which is slightly better than the
No Information Rate of 55.7%. This No Information Rate represents the
performance of a basic model that predicts “Republican” for every
paragraph. However, this improvement isn’t statistically significant (as
p = 0.19), meaning that we can’t claim with full confidence that the
model is doing better than chance. The confusion matrix makes the
picture concrete: the model misclassifies 75 Democrat paragraphs as
Republican, and 50 Republican paragraphs as Democrat.
The asymmetry between parties is noteworthy. When the model predicts
Republican it is more often correct (Precision: 64.8%), but it catches a
greater share of the actual Democrat paragraphs (Recall: 62.4%) — at the
cost of more false positives. The F1-score of 57.0% highlights this
uneven trade-off in a single number.
Despite the keyness analysis highlighting clear group-level
differences in partisan vocabulary, however, the classifier struggles to
translate those patterns into reliable paragraph-level predictions. This
gap between description and prediction is itself a meaningful finding:
partisan language differences exist, however, they are too subtle and
variable for a bag-of-words model to exploit reliably at the paragraph
level. The three limitations identified — 160 years of linguistic drift,
paragraphs that are not truly independent of each other, and only 41
speeches at the document level — are all likely contributors.
Nonetheless, this project demonstrates the complete text analysis
pipeline: from loading and labelling a corpus, through preprocessing and
keyness analysis, to supervised classification and honest evaluation.
Rather than overstating what a simple model can achieve, the analysis
arrives at a result that is transparent about its own limitations —
which is, ultimately, what good quantitative research looks like.
